2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Some concerns / Moderate risk: Actual post-order latrine installation and customer cancellation rates were completely unmeasured because follow-up ended at the conclusion of the 7.5-month sales period; the authors note that 10–20% of orders are typically cancelled prior to installation (pp. 8–9), which could plausibly differ between subsidized and unsubsidized buyers. In addition, 1,598 repeat-visit records (including 36 sales) were excluded post hoc from the analytic dataset (p. 4, Footnote 17), and household non-contact/refusal denominators during village canvassing were not reported.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Low-to-moderate concern: Computer-generated village-level randomization across 30 clusters stratified by commune climate vulnerability status, supported by baseline cluster balance checks and village-clustered regressions controlling for climate vulnerability (pp. 4–5), protects village-level intent-to-treat estimates against baseline cluster confounding. However, post-randomization differential recruitment of IDPoor/eligible households within treatment villages (pp. 6–7, 9) introduces within-cluster selection/confounding risk for household-level comparisons, and comparisons between eligible and ineligible subgroups are non-randomized.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate / Moderate concern: The subsidy targeting rule integrates two official Cambodian administrative classifications—the government IDPoor proxy-means poverty registry and commune-level Climate Vulnerability Index (CVI) scores from the National Council for Sustainable Development—with the country-validated 10-item Cambodia Poverty Probability Index (PPI) and a fixed 50% price discount (pp. 2–4). However, exact CVI score cutoffs and PPI eligibility thresholds are relegated to Supporting Information rather than presented in the main text (pp. 3–4), household-level climate shock relied on a subjective unverified 1-year self-report question (p. 9), and qualitative interviews revealed persistent misunderstandings of the eligibility rules among trained sales agents and village leaders (p. 9).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Some concerns / Moderate risk: Sales agents collecting eligibility and sales-order data were unblinded to cluster assignment and received sales commissions (pp. 4, 9). Household climate vulnerability was measured via a single subjective self-reported 1-year shock question vulnerable to differential interpretation or strategic reporting (p. 9), and independent M&E verification re-assessments covered approximately 10% of purchasing households only, excluding non-purchasing households (p. 4).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak-to-moderate (Some concerns): Although framed around access to climate-resilient sanitation, the study measured only point-of-pitch latrine purchase orders ('sales closing rate') rather than verified latrine delivery, physical installation, structural flood resilience, or household toilet use, explicitly omitting an estimated 10–20% order cancellation rate (pp. 8–9).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Some concerns: No trial registration or pre-analysis plan is reported anywhere in the article. Main-text statistical reporting is incomplete—Table 1 presents marginal probabilities and p-values ('0.00') without sample sizes, standard errors, or confidence intervals, while balance checks and village-level regression tables are deferred to Supporting Information (pp. 4, 6). Post-hoc dropping of 1,598 duplicate visits (p. 4, Footnote 17) and minor internal numerical discrepancies across pages (treatment eligibility reported as 51% on p. 6 vs. 'close to 52%' on p. 7; subsidized repeat-visit buyers reported as 26 [1%] on p. 7 vs. 29 [2%] on p. 9) raise additional reporting concerns.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High risk: Although cluster allocation across the 30 villages was computer-randomized and stratified (p. 4), households were identified and approached after randomization by unblinded sales agents assisted by unblinded village authorities, restricted to households without a toilet where a decisionmaker was home (p. 4). Village authorities in treatment clusters were substantially more supportive in identifying poor households, producing a statistically significant imbalance in subsidy eligibility (51–52% in treatment vs. 45% in control, p = 0.00) driven by a 5 percentage point higher share of IDPoor households in treatment areas (p = 0.00), which the authors explicitly recognize as selection bias (pp. 6–7, 9).

domain_ratings.justification: Treatment assignment was randomly allocated simultaneously across the 30 study villages (15 treatment, 15 control) using a computer-generated sequence (Stata's randtreat function), stratified by commune-level climate vulnerability status (23 climate-vulnerable villages split 12 treatment and 11 control). Cluster-level balance checks were performed across key baseline variables to confirm no statistically significant differences between arms (though the full balance table is located in Supporting Information rather than the main text).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters
domain_ratings.justification: Individual households were not enumerated prior to village randomization; instead, unblinded sales agents entered randomized villages and approached households without a toilet (so long as a decisionmaker was home) with the assistance of unblinded local village authorities. Qualitative interviews and administrative data confirmed that village authorities in subsidy (treatment) villages were much more inclined to help identify poor and unlatrined households, and sales commissions incentivized targeting eligible buyers. Consequently, subsidy eligibility was significantly higher in treatment than control villages (51–52% vs. 45%, p = 0.00), driven by a 5 percentage point higher proportion of IDPoor households in treatment clusters (p = 0.00), which the authors explicitly acknowledge as selection bias.

domain_ratings.justification: Because the intervention consisted of offering a 50% latrine price discount during door-to-door sales pitches, neither households, sales agents, nor village leaders were blinded. During the 7.5-month rollout, sales agents made 1,598 repeat/duplicate household visits (yielding 36 sales), which analysts subsequently dropped post hoc from the dataset to approximate single-visit selling conditions. Qualitative interviews also revealed persistent misunderstandings among trained sales agents and village leaders regarding how the PPI and climate thresholds operated, although automated/structured scoring and independent M&E spot-checks of ~10% of purchasing households identified no willful manipulation. Village-level randomization helped prevent cross-arm spillover.

domain_ratings.justification: For the analyzed point-of-sale purchase order variable among first-visit consented presentations (n = 2,821), immediate pitch outcomes were recorded, but the paper does not report village-level denominators of unlatrined households missed because no decisionmaker was home or who declined consent, and 1,598 duplicate-visit records (including 36 sales) were excluded post hoc. Crucially, follow-up ended immediately after the sales window without tracking order cancellations or actual latrine installations; the authors note typical cancellation rates of 10–20% in iDE programs, leaving actual sanitation uptake incomplete and potentially subject to differential cancellation between subsidized and full-price orders.

domain_ratings.justification: Outcomes were recorded by unblinded, commission-paid iDE sales agents as sales orders ('sales closing rate') rather than independently verified latrine installations (ignoring an estimated 10–20% cancellation rate). raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Study S057 (Kozole et al., 2023) is a 30-village cluster-randomized controlled trial in Kampong Chhnang province, rural Cambodia (2,821 unique household sales presentations), supplemented by 13 stakeholder interviews and a programmatic cost analysis, evaluating whether a climate- and poverty-targeted 50% price subsidy (combining Cambodia's IDPoor registry, commune Climate Vulnerability Index [CVI], and household Poverty Probability Index [PPI] plus self-reported climate shocks) increases sales conversion for resilient latrines. Appraised with the RoB 2 cluster-randomized trials variant, the study has an overall High risk of bias. While village-level randomization was properly executed via Stata's randtreat stratified on commune climate vulnerability with baseline balance checks (D1a: Low), household identification and recruitment occurred post-randomization through unblinded sales agents and village authorities (D1b: High). As confirmed by both administrative data and qualitative agent interviews, village authorities in treatment clusters provided greater support in locating poor, unlatrined households, producing a statistically significant excess of subsidy-eligible (51–52% vs. 45%, p = 0.00) and IDPoor (+5 percentage points, p = 0.00) households in treatment villages. Additional Some concerns arise across D2–D5: unblinded implementation involved 1,598 repeat visits that were dropped post hoc alongside persistent agent misunderstandings of PPI scoring rules (D2); post-order follow-up was truncated before installation, omitting typical 10–20% order cancellation rates and unreported household non-contact/refusal denominators (D3); outcomes captured unblinded agent-recorded latrine orders rather than verified installations, with M&E spot-checks restricted to ~10% of buyers and subjective self-reported household climate shocks (D4); and no trial registration or pre-analysis plan was reported alongside sparse main-text statistical reporting and minor numerical inconsistencies across sections (D5).
raw_response.study_design_identified: Cluster-randomized controlled trial (30 villages randomized 1:1 to targeted 50% sanitation subsidy vs. retail-price control, stratified by commune climate vulnerability; n = 2,821 unique household sales presentations) with ancillary qualitative stakeholder interviews (n = 13) and pilot cost-effectiveness analysis

raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study's core empirical causal design is a cluster-randomized controlled trial in which 30 rural Cambodian villages (clusters) were randomized 1:1 via Stata's randtreat function to receive targeted 50% sanitation subsidies or retail-price sales pitches, evaluating household- and village-level latrine sales conversion (pp. 2, 4–5). Although the authors also conducted 13 qualitative stakeholder interviews and a cost-scaling exercise to contextualize implementation and market distortion (pp. 4, 6–8), the paper frames its primary design as a clustered RCT, presents no standalone qualitative themes table or verbatim interview quotes in Results, and exhibits textbook post-randomization within-cluster participant recruitment issues that only the RoB 2 cluster-randomized trials variant (Domain D1b) is specifically designed to evaluate.
